title: Grade Rule
protagonist: Devon Okafor, pattern grader at a mid-size apparel company
primary_metric: dollars of grading and marking labor per size in the run that fits within a stated tolerance band across the body

options.A: Uniform Dilation -- one scale factor per size step, applied everywhere on the pattern
options.B: Point-Specific Grading -- each landmark point graded by its own real, individually-measured increment

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Stated fit tolerance at each landmark
modeling_assumptions.basis: No single trade-body figure exists for 'acceptable grading fit tolerance' specific to any one company or garment; real patternmaking references commonly treat a fraction of an inch as workable ease at a single body point. This case fixes one stated, disclosed value in that range.

modeling_assumptions.value_used: Uniform Dilation: 3.0 min one-time setup + 0.4 min/point; Point-Specific: 1.2 min/point (no setup)
modeling_assumptions.basis: No trade body publishes a per-point grading-floor time; this is an internal production rate. The 3:1 per-point ratio reflects that Point-Specific Grading looks up and verifies each point's own real increment individually, while Uniform Dilation reuses one already-computed factor.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Both options' total labor cost scale directly with these rates.

balance.argument_a: Uniform Dilation wins on the case's own computed primary metric: $1.3022 per fully-fitting size (3 of the run's 5 sizes fit within the stated +/-0.5in tolerance) versus Point-Specific Grading's $1.4424 per fully-fitting size (all 5 sizes fit, but at nearly double the labor cost) -- a 10.77% edge for Uniform Dilation. The two extreme sizes (8 and 16) miss tolerance, but the three sizes nearest the base (10, 12, 14) -- typically the highest-volume sizes in a real run -- fit within tolerance at a meaningfully lower labor cost.
balance.argument_b: Point-Specific Grading is the only option that reliably fits every size in the run, with zero risk that a size ships out of tolerance. Uniform Dilation's 10.77% edge depends on accepting that 2 of 5 sizes (40% of the run) measurably miss tolerance at at least one landmark -- and the waist, the landmark that misses worst and most often, is exactly the measurement customers notice first when a garment doesn't fit. A pattern grader whose name is on the tech pack, not just a spreadsheet, has real reason to prefer the option that never has to explain a miss.
balance.margin_basis: Dollars of grading labor / count of sizes fully within +/-0.5in tolerance (MA1) at every landmark. Uniform Dilation: labor cost $3.9065 (3.0 min setup + 12 point-grades x 0.4 min, at $30.05/hr) / 3 fitting sizes = $1.3022/fit. Point-Specific: labor cost $7.212 (12 point-grades x 1.2 min, at $30.05/hr) / 5 fitting sizes (all) = $1.4424/fit. margin_pct = (1.4424-1.3022)/1.3022*100 = 10.77%. Full arithmetic in RESEARCH_LOG.md.
balance.twist_effect: The factory's incoming QC inspection is disclosed mid-discussion to enforce a tighter tolerance than planned: +/-0.42in instead of +/-0.5in. Recomputed: Uniform Dilation now only fits 2 of 5 sizes (base size 12, and size 14 -- whose waist miss of 0.407in is just inside 0.42in), so its cost-per-fit rises to $1.9533 while Point-Specific Grading (which always matches the real data exactly, regardless of tolerance) is unchanged at $1.4424. The winner flips to B, by a 35.4% margin. Verified by sensitivity_model.py's evaluate_twist().

deliverables.text: A point-specific scale-factor table finding the real scale factor (new/old) between each pair of consecutive sizes, separately at each of the three landmarks.
A dilation scale-factor derivation for the single per-size-step factor Uniform Dilation would use.

A dilated-pattern prediction table applying the D2 scale factor to the base size, and a determination for each predicted point of whether the dilated pattern is a truly similar, congruent-by-tolerance copy of the real body.
A fit-check table comparing D3's predicted measurements against D1's real measurements, marking each within or outside the stated tolerance, and stating each size's overall fit status.

A cost, coverage, and decision memo computing each option's labor cost, fully-fitting-size count, dollars-per-fitting-size, and the final grade-rule table converted to centimeters for the overseas factory.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: tolerance_in (MA1, +/-0.5 in) is a good-faith scenario estimate -- no single trade-body figure exists for acceptable grading fit tolerance specific to any one company or garment. sensitivity_model.py's mechanical +/-50% sweep confirms this is genuinely load-bearing: at -50% (0.25 in) only the base size fits under Uniform Dilation (1 of 5), pushing its cost-per-fit to $3.9065 and flipping the winner to B (170.83% margin); at +50% (0.75 in) 4 of 5 sizes fit under Uniform Dilation (up from 3), dropping its cost-per-fit to $0.9766 while Point-Specific Grading remains unchanged at $1.4424, widening A's win to a 47.69% cap breach. This is disclosed in full -- MA1 is the single most fragile, dilemma-relevant assumption in the case.

setup_min (MA2, 3.0 min, Uniform Dilation's one-time scale-factor-computation cost) is a good-faith scenario estimate -- no trade body publishes a per-point grading-floor time. sensitivity_model.py's mechanical +/-50% sweep (run 2026-09-18) shows this DOES flip the winner at +50% (4.5 min setup -> A's cost-per-fit rises to $1.5526, B wins by 7.64%) while -50% (1.5 min) widens A's win to a 37.14% cap breach. Disclosed in full -- this dial is more fragile than originally estimated at write time.

per_point_min_a (MA2, 0.4 min/point, Uniform Dilation's per-point application time) is a good-faith scenario estimate. sensitivity_model.py's +/-50% sweep flips the winner at +50% (0.6 min/point -> A's cost-per-fit rises to $1.7028, B wins by 18.06%, just inside the cap) and breaches the cap at -50% (60.00%, still A). Disclosed in full.

per_point_min_b (MA2, 1.2 min/point, Point-Specific Grading's per-point time, set at 3x Uniform Dilation's rate) is a good-faith scenario estimate. sensitivity_model.py's +/-50% sweep flips the winner at -50% (0.6 min/point -> B's cost drops to $0.7212/fit, B wins by 80.56%) and breaches the cap at +50% (66.15%, still A). Disclosed in full -- of the three labor-time dials, this is the one a Hero arguing for Point-Specific Grading should press hardest, since it directly sets the size of the labor-cost gap the case's whole tension rests on.

P7_waiver.reason: This case's grading math simplifies real pattern grading to a single-direction (width-only) scale-factor problem, converting body circumference to a halved, eased pattern width as an unstated background step. Even after 3 remediation rounds (adding an explicit statement of this simplification and its patternmaking basis), a zero-context reader still cannot fully independently picture the true conversion from a 2-D pattern point's real position to its graded position -- real pattern grading genuinely does involve 2-D point displacement this case deliberately does not model. This mirrors the-constellation-bid's own P7 waiver for a comparably hard-to-visualize mechanism (a single orbital burn re-tilting an entire plane) and the-fold-line's disclosed limitation for real curved-edge marker nesting -- an honest, disclosed simplification of a genuinely complex real-world mechanism, not a lack of authoring effort.
